proxy_language: Modern-era Pan-African culinary/court lexicon, proxied by Yoruba (Standard Yoruba orthography) with Akan (Twi) and Hausa as secondary donors
proxy_rationale: 'Eolaskumlacht' is not a recognizable historical culture or attested language, and the string itself is not a real word in any language I can verify. The sample names (Jollof, Egusi, Fufu, Suya, Waakye, Akara) are West African foodways from Wolof/Mandinka (jollof), Yoruba (egusi, akara in Yoruba/Hausa as akara/kosai), Akan (fufu, waakye), and Hausa (suya, tsire). A defensible proxy for a worldwide-network later-court culture whose naming is dominated by West African food and trade is Yoruba, the best-documented large West African language with a standard orthography, supplemented by Akan and Hausa. This is a proxy choice, not an identification of the culture. The name itself should not be treated as Irish or Goidelic.
phonology: Standard Yoruba: consonants b, t, d, k, g, gb /k\u0361p/, f, s, \u1e63 /\u0283/, h, j, l, r, m, n, w, y, p. Seven oral vowels a, e, \u1eb9 /\u025b/, i, o, \u1ecd /\u0254/, u, plus nasalized vowels (in, an, un, \u1ecdn, \u1eb9n written as vowel + n). Three level tones: high (acute), mid (unmarked), low (grave). No consonant clusters; no vowel length contrast. Akan donor items add labialized and palatalized series (kw, tw, hw, dw, ky, ny) and vowel harmony.
phonotactics: Open syllables only: (C)V or syllabic nasal (N). Syllable shapes V, CV, N. No codas except a syllabic nasal or the nasal of a nasalized vowel. No consonant clusters inside a syllable; gb and kp count as single consonants. Words commonly begin with a vowel (nouns often have an initial vowel, e.g. \u1eb9ja 'fish', ar\u00f9n 'illness', \u00ecw\u00e9 'book'). Tone is lexical and is normally not written in game-friendly Latin text, so the audit should allow but not require tone diacritics. Loans from Hausa/Akan may be reshaped to open syllables.
orthography: Standard Yoruba Latin orthography: subdot letters \u1eb9, \u1ecd, \u1e63; digraph gb; tone marks (acute, grave) and optional macron-free mid tone; nasal vowels as V+n. For game use, an ASCII-friendly variant (e, o, s for \u1eb9, \u1ecd, \u1e63) is acceptable. Hausa donor spelling: b, \u0253, d, \u0257, \u0199, ts, sh, ' for glottal stop, ai/au diphthongs. Akan donor spelling: \u025b, \u0254, ky, tw, hw, ny, nk, nt, nd clusters of nasal+stop.
morphology: Yoruba is isolating with little inflection. Nouns often carry a vowel prefix (a-, \u00e0-, \u00ec-, \u00f2-, \u1eb9-, \u1ecd-, o-, \u00e8-) forming agent, instrument, or abstract nouns from verbs: o-/\u1ecd-/a- agentive (\u1ecdl\u1ecdd\u00e0 'owner of ...'), \u00ec-/\u00e0- abstract (\u00ecj\u1ecdba 'kingship'). Verb-noun nominalization uses reduplication of the verb with prefix \u00e8-/\u00ec- (\u00e8k\u1ecd 'lesson/pap' from k\u1ecd 'teach'). Plural is expressed with words such as \u00e0w\u1ecdn 'they/the' or by context. No case or gender. Honorific and praise-name (or\u00ed, \u00e8sa) formation is a major naming resource.
compounding: Nouns compose head-first: head noun then modifier, with genitive constructions formed by juxtaposition (possessed noun first, possessor second: il\u00e9 \u1ecdba 'house of the king' = palace). 'X of Y': X + Y with no linker, sometimes with a mid-toned linker n\u00ed or ti in fuller phrases. 'Y-maker/seller': a- or o- agent prefix + verb + object (onis\u00e9\u0301\u00f2g\u00f9n?) and the common pattern oni- 'owner/seller of' + noun (on\u00ed\u00e8wa 'bean seller', aladi\u00fa 'palm-oil seller'): oni-/ol\u00f3-/al\u00e1- + noun. Verb-object compounds (\u00e0-g\u00ed 'cutter') also occur.
noun_phrase_order: Head noun first, then adjective, then demonstrative or numeral: \u1eb9ja ki\u1e63\u00ed 'big fish' type order (noun + adjective), possessor after possessed (il\u00e9 \u1ecdba), demonstratives follow the noun (il\u00e9 y\u00ec\u00ed 'this house'). Akan and Hausa donors: Akan noun + adjective; Hausa noun + genitive linker -n/-r (gidan sarki 'the king's house').

notes: No word may be identical to a Modern Irish, Scottish Gaelic or Manx word, since the proxy is not Goidelic. 'Eolaskumlacht' is not an attested culture or language; it resembles Irish-style spelling (eolas 'knowledge') but is not Irish, and the audit should not treat it as a model. The forbidden-patterns set enforces open syllables: no triple consonants, no lone medial consonant without a following vowel, no c/q/v/x/z, and no consonant-final words except syllabic n/m. Because Yoruba subdot letters may not survive all pipelines, accept ASCII e/o/s as equivalents. Treat all Hausa and Akan items as donor flavor only, reshaped to open syllables.
